source: Li & Kingsford (2026) Means-Ends Analysis Helps LLMs Plan in Continuous-State Domains (MEDAKA, LiquidWorld)
finding: First direct test of a means-ends prompt on LLMs. MEDAKA prompts for recursive goal decomposition, algebraic derivation and per-step state tracking. It beat plain chain of thought (CoT) and AoT+ (search-in-prompt) on a liquid-mixing planning testbed for most models.
numbers: Total pass@1 (CoT / AoT+ / MEDAKA), 3 rollouts per problem, thinking mode off: Claude-Sonnet-4.6 77.8/85.0/94.5; Gemini-3-Flash 65.6/71.6/82.0; GPT-5.4 74.3/78.5/78.5; GPT-4o 25.7/19.8/36.9; LLaMA-3.3-70B 26.6/17.6/40.6; Gemma4-4B 55.7/52.7/61.0; Gemma4-2B 26.3/23.8/30.5.
quote: classical means-ends analysis elicits LLM-native reasoning abilities that are helpful for continuous-state planning
limits: Authors' own new testbed, no independent replication, preprint. Thinking mode was disabled for all models, so gain over reasoning models is unknown. GPT-5.4 gained nothing overall.
agent_relevance: Direct support for O5: a gap-then-operator-then-precondition-as-subgoal loop with explicit state update after every step lifts weaker and mid models most.

source: Li & Kingsford (2026) Means-Ends Analysis Helps LLMs Plan in Continuous-State Domains (MEDAKA, LiquidWorld)
finding: The gain is largest on hard structure: nonlinear constraints, coupled parameters, many goals, distractors. Frontier models were already saturated on linear problems.
numbers: Nonlinear pass@1 CoT/AoT+/MEDAKA: Claude 33.3/55.3/87.4; Gemini 16.4/21.4/50.9; GPT-5.4 28.9/49.1/46.5 (MEDAKA below AoT+). Multi-goal Claude 50.4 to 89.5 (CoT to MEDAKA). Distractor vessels Claude 73.8 to 94.0; GPT-4o 10.7 to 42.9. Linear Claude 95.1/96.6/97.3.
limits: On nonlinear problems the open-weight models did not gain (e.g. Gemma4-4B 14.5/15.1/12.6). Gains do not appear on every model.
agent_relevance: Means-ends structure pays off when subgoals interact and the state is long. Do not force it on easy single-step items (supports guardrail G1).

source: Li & Kingsford (2026) Means-Ends Analysis Helps LLMs Plan in Continuous-State Domains (MEDAKA, LiquidWorld)
finding: Ablation of the two MEDAKA parts: dropping either recursive decomposition or per-step state tracking lowers pass@1, so both contribute.
numbers: Full MEDAKA Claude 94.5, Gemini 82.0. Removing state tracking or removing the recursive module: Claude 90.5 (-4.0) and 91.0 (-3.5); Gemini 76.0 (-6.0) and 75.1 (-6.9). Row-to-column mapping of the Gemini pair was garbled in the text extraction.
limits: Only two models, 3 trials each. Contributions need not be additive (each ablation keeps one module). Even the ablated variants beat CoT (Claude 77.8, Gemini 65.6).
agent_relevance: Decomposition alone gives part of the gain, state tracking after each operator gives the rest. Both belong in the S-state loop.

source: Li & Kingsford (2026) Means-Ends Analysis Helps LLMs Plan in Continuous-State Domains (MEDAKA, LiquidWorld)
finding: Failure modes of search-style prompts (AoT+) in continuous domains: trial-and-error parameter guessing, state hallucination and drift, and locally correct but globally inconsistent arithmetic (fixing one component at a time).
numbers: Example: goal 4 L at (36.71, 26.67, 36.62)%; plan reached 4 L at (36.7, 40.0, 23.3)% because each pour fixed one component and disturbed another. Another trace emptied vessel V8 then reused it as if full.
limits: Qualitative, inspected only on GPT-4o and LLaMA-3.3-70B linear problems.
agent_relevance: This is the classic means-ends weakness (fixing one difference reintroduces another). Code should check the full goal vector after every operator.

source: Li & Kingsford (2026) Means-Ends Analysis Helps LLMs Plan in Continuous-State Domains (MEDAKA, LiquidWorld)
finding: Cost check: MEDAKA uses 1.8 to 3.8 times the tokens of CoT (median), so it was compared to best-of-3 CoT. Even so its single try beat CoT best-of-3 on 4 of 7 models.
numbers: Claude: CoT pass@3 86.8 vs MEDAKA pass@1 94.5. Gemini: 67.2 vs 82.0. Exceptions: GPT-5.4 and both Gemma4 models.
limits: Compute-matched only against oracle best-of-3, not against majority voting.
agent_relevance: Structured subgoal prompts can use extra tokens better than resampling plain CoT (G4: samples from one model are correlated).

source: Mondal, Webb et al. (2023/2025, Nature Communications) Improving Planning with LLMs: A Modular Agentic Architecture (MAP)
finding: MAP gives GPT-4 a TaskDecomposer (one subgoal at a time, using a recursive goal strategy: move the smallest blocked disk, first clear larger disks in the way), plus Actor, Monitor, Predictor, Evaluator and Orchestrator. On a text-only isomorphic Tower of Hanoi it solved far more than plain GPT-4.
numbers: ToH 3 disks, percent solved without invalid moves: MAP 74 (100 on best of 5 runs); GPT-4 zero-shot about 11; nearly seven-fold gain. 4-disk (out of distribution): baselines near 0%, MAP 0 invalid moves. Mean plan length 5.4 vs optimal 4.4.
quote: MAP's improved performance relative to MAD demonstrates the importance of interaction between specialized LLM instances
limits: Single run per baseline (deterministic), GPT-4 only for the main result, 3-disk puzzle is small. Isomorphic text version was meant to avoid training-data recall.
agent_relevance: Subgoal proposal as a separate, narrow module (not the same model free-running) is a tested pattern for O5.

source: Mondal, Webb et al. (2023/2025, Nature Communications) Improving Planning with LLMs: A Modular Agentic Architecture (MAP)
finding: Ablation on 3-disk ToH: the Monitor (rule check of proposed moves) mattered most, then tree search, then the TaskDecomposer.
numbers: Percent solved (best of 5 in brackets): MAP 74 (100); no TaskDecomposer 50 (67); no tree search 32 (42); no Monitor 27 (33) with 31% invalid moves vs 0% for the others.
limits: 3-disk only. Decomposer removal cost 24 points, so subgoaling helps but a validity check helps more.
agent_relevance: Matches G2/G3: a separate validity check outweighs the subgoal proposer. Do not trust the model to keep to the rules.

source: Mondal, Webb et al. (2023/2025, Nature Communications) Improving Planning with LLMs: A Modular Agentic Architecture (MAP)
finding: Giving the baselines the same goal-recursion strategy that MAP's decomposer gets helps them but does not close the gap. Strategy knowledge alone is not the explanation.
numbers: ToH 3 disks, percent solved: GPT-4 zero-shot 11 and 23 with goal recursion; MAP 74. Other rows of Table 12 (ICL, CoT) were garbled in the text extraction. Search depth L=2 was the best trade-off; a Llama3-70B version of MAP still beat GPT-4 ICL.
limits: Table partly unreadable in the extraction; only the zero-shot pair is certain.
agent_relevance: Telling the model the means-ends recipe in the prompt is weaker than enforcing it with separate calls and checks.

source: Mondal, Webb et al. (2023/2025, Nature Communications) Improving Planning with LLMs: A Modular Agentic Architecture (MAP)
finding: MAP on PlanBench roughly doubled to tripled plain GPT-4 on the hardest obfuscated domain, and showed some transfer to unseen planning tasks.
numbers: PlanBench percent solved (zero-shot / ICL / CoT / MAP): Logistics 7/12/17/24; Mystery Blocksworld 0.2/7.8/10.6/27.4. Transfer (ICL/CoT/MAP): n7tree to n15star 0.2/1.4/12.2. On a subset: Logistics MAP 53.3 vs ToT 10.4 (30 problems); Mystery BW MAP 35 vs ToT 0.6 (100 problems).
limits: Logistics and Mystery BW still mostly unsolved (24%, 27%). Other transfer cells ambiguous in extraction. MAP ran without tree search on PlanBench because of cost.
agent_relevance: Structured subgoal and monitor loops help on obfuscated domains where pattern matching fails, but absolute levels stay low.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) The Illusion of Thinking (Apple), Tower of Hanoi results
finding: Reasoning models solve Tower of Hanoi at small N, then accuracy falls to near zero from about N=8, and thinking-token use also drops near the cliff. Giving the full recursive algorithm in the prompt did not move the collapse point.
numbers: Easy N=1-4: correct answer found early then overthinking. N=5-7: correct found late. N>=8: near-zero accuracy. Claude-3.7-Thinking near-perfect at N=5 (31 moves) yet fails River Crossing at N=3 (11 moves). In ToH N=10 first error around move 100. Algorithm-given runs collapsed at roughly the same point (Fig 8).
quote: even when we provide the algorithm in the prompt... performance does not improve
limits: Contested (next line): token limits, move-list output format, unsolvable River Crossing instances. Not a means-ends study as such; ToH is solved by a fixed recursion.
agent_relevance: Knowing the subgoal recursion is not the same as executing it for hundreds of steps. Execution needs external state and checks, not a better recipe in the prompt.

source: Lawsen (2025) The Illusion of the Illusion of Thinking
finding: Comment on the Apple paper: much of the ToH collapse is an output-format and token-limit artefact. Asking for a generating function instead of a full move list restored high accuracy at N=15.
numbers: Corrected count of 10 tokens per move; a full list for N=15 is 32,767 moves. Preliminary test with a Lua-function prompt on Claude 3.7, Opus 4, o3 and Gemini 2.5: very high accuracy in under 5,000 tokens. River Crossing instances with N>=6 are impossible with the stated boat capacity.
quote: Scoring models as failures for making reasonable engineering decisions about output length mischaracterizes their actual capabilities
limits: Preliminary, few models, no accuracy table, partly relies on a social-media replication. The author's original token arithmetic had a slip, corrected in v2.
agent_relevance: The model can state the means-ends recursion as code. Let the program, not the model, emit the long move list (matches the schema split of who does what).

source: Pereira & Zuidema (2026) Transformers Struggle to Use Their Emergent World Models: Revisiting the Tower of Hanoi and the Illusion of Thinking
finding: 2026 models solve the standard tower-to-tower puzzle near-perfectly, so the famous collapse is gone. The harder flat-to-flat variant (start and goal both spread across pegs, no memorised recursion) is still hard: about half solved optimally, falling with disk count.
numbers: Tower-to-tower n=3-5: DeepSeek-R1 24/25, Kimi-K2-Think 23/25, gpt-oss-120b 25/25, Qwen3.6-27B 24/25, R1-Distill-Qwen-32B 1/25. Flat-to-flat optimal solves out of 100 (n=3-5): DeepSeek-R1 40, Kimi-K2 25, gpt-oss-120b 51, Qwen3.6-27B 51, R1-Distill 7. Qwen3.6-27B by n: 28/34, 14/33, 9/33, 4/33 (n=6), 2/33 (n=7).
quote: the optimal path depends on the pair (sI , sG) and cannot be produced by a memorised recursive template
limits: Master-thesis-based preprint, 32k answer-token cap, prompt from Shojaee et al.
agent_relevance: Flat-to-flat is the real means-ends test: choose which difference to attack first. Even strong models fail it, so the subgoal-order choice (O5) needs help.

source: Pereira & Zuidema (2026) Transformers Struggle to Use Their Emergent World Models (steering experiments)
finding: Probes show the model encodes the puzzle state well at the prompt, but the encoding degrades during the long chain of thought. Pushing the state representation back to the clean one (activation steering) turned many failures into optimal solutions.
numbers: Qwen3.6-27B: optimal solves on 81 configurations 33 (41%) to 59 (73%) at best steering strength; weakest setting converts 52% of failures; 26 of 48 failures fixed at best vs 6 of 72 for R1-Distill-32B. Probe fidelity was the same for a 27B model and a 6-layer transformer trained from scratch.
limits: Needs open weights and white-box access; not usable on API models. Non-monotonic in steering strength.
agent_relevance: Causal evidence that state drift mid-trace is the failure, not the planning idea. Supports re-stating and re-reading the true state after every operator (per-step state tracking in MEDAKA).

source: Meyerson et al. (2025) Solving a Million-Step LLM Task with Zero Errors (MAKER)
finding: Solved 20-disk Tower of Hanoi (over one million dependent steps) with zero errors by splitting into single-step subtasks, voting (first-to-ahead-by-k) and discarding malformed outputs. The solving strategy is supplied in every prompt, so this tests execution, not choice of subgoals.
numbers: 20 disks = 2^20 - 1 = 1,048,575 steps; gpt-4.1-mini, k_min=3, output cap 750 tokens, temperature 0 for first vote then 0.1. Per-step error rate 0.0022 to 0.0045 for gpt-4.1-mini and did not rise with disks. Two independent runs on 10K samples: zero steps wrong in both.
quote: The approach relies on an extreme decomposition of a task into subtasks, each of which can be tackled by focused microagents
limits: Strategy is given, so subgoal discovery is not tested. Authors say automatic discovery of decompositions is open. Vendor-lab preprint.
agent_relevance: Once the means-ends plan is fixed, each step is cheap and checkable. Vote only at the execution layer. Errors were decorrelated here.

source: Meyerson et al. (2025) MAKER, per-model cost table
finding: Cheap non-reasoning models were more cost-effective than reasoning models for step execution. Per-step error rates and projected cost to solve the 20-disk task at 95% success varied by two orders of magnitude.
numbers: Projected cost: gpt-4.1-nano error 0.357, k_min 29, about $41.9K; gpt-4.1-mini (temp 0.1) error 0.0022, k_min 3, $3.5K; o3-mini low error 0.0018, $9.4K; haiku-4.5 error 0.184, $71.2K; gpt-oss-20B error 0.0358, $1.7K; llama-3.2-3B error 1.0 (cannot vote).
limits: Projection, not billed totals. Error rates from 10K samples. One task type.
agent_relevance: Choose the cheapest model whose per-step error is below about 0.5% when steps are verified by code.

source: Su et al. (2025) Limits of Emergent Reasoning of LLMs in Agentic Frameworks for Deterministic Games
finding: Removing the state-tracking burden (a tool interface that returns the board after each move) did not remove the Tower of Hanoi collapse. It made it appear earlier, with the model stuck in loops.
numbers: Claude 3.7 Sonnet and DeepSeek V3.1/R1, up to 8 disks. In the agentic setting about 40% of the time the model deterministically reused previously seen continuations at n=8. Policy drifts away from both the optimal and the uniform-random policy as n grows.
quote: access to an environment interface does not delay or eradicate performance collapse
limits: Small study, figures only, no accuracy table in text. One puzzle.
agent_relevance: Counter-evidence: handing back the true state is not enough. A loop detector and a rule that forbids repeating a state are needed (G1 impasse signal).

source: Utsho et al. (2026) Empirical Evidence of Complexity-Induced Limits in LLMs on Finite Discrete State-Space Problems
finding: Nine puzzle families with exact validators show a phase-transition style collapse as size grows. On Tower of Hanoi all models solve levels 1 and 2, differ at level 3, and at level 4 all collapse except Gemini 3 Pro and DeepSeek V3.2.
numbers: Water jug: all perfect through level 3, only Gemini 3 Pro succeeds at level 4. Many tasks show accuracy drops above 50 points beyond a task-specific threshold. Hanoi, a template-friendly task, held up longest.
limits: Qualitative reading from figures; model list and exact levels vary by task. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Template tasks (Hanoi) are weak tests of means-ends choice. Pick benchmarks where subgoals interact.

source: Futuhi & Sturtevant (2026) Planning with Transformers: Chain of Computation and Structured Context Windows
finding: Small transformers trained from scratch inside an outer loop (one operator application per call, structured context holding only what the step needs) learn planning procedures and exceed 99% on BlocksWorld and the Pancake puzzle. A pushdown-automaton form handles Tower of Hanoi up to 20 disks.
numbers: >99% success on BlocksWorld and Pancake puzzle; ToH up to 20 disks; trained from a small number of instances.
limits: Trained models, not prompted frontier LLMs. The recursive Hanoi procedure is supplied through training traces. Abstract and method outline read; training details not checked.
agent_relevance: A one-operator-per-call loop with constant-size context is the same shape as the schema's program-driven transitions.

source: Wang et al. (2026) A Subgoal-driven Framework for Improving Long-Horizon LLM Agents (Google DeepMind; SGO and MiRA)
finding: Online subgoal decomposition with a milestone checklist and a self-check against the current screen raised Gemini-2.5-pro on WebArena-Lite. Milestone-based dense reward then raised Gemma3-12B from 6.4% to 43.0%.
numbers: Gemini-2.5-pro 23.0% to 32.1% success (about +9 to +10 points). Stuck-midway errors 48.41% (Pro) to 39.87% with SGO; wrong terminations 9.52% to 12.03%. Gemma3-12B + MiRA 43.0% vs WebRL 35.1% and DigiRL 33.3% (Gemma3), GPT-4-Turbo 17.6%, GPT-4o 13.9%.
limits: Web navigation, one benchmark (WebArena-Lite), vendor authors. Table columns were jumbled in extraction; headline numbers taken from the text.
agent_relevance: A subgoal checklist plus a verify-before-advance step reduced stalls. Check each subgoal against the real state, not the model's belief.

source: Wang et al. (2026) MiRA ablation
finding: Training ablation: without the potential critic (subgoal-based shaping) learning plateaus near 35%, close to the plain RL level; the full method reaches 43%.
numbers: MiRA full about 31% to 43% across phases; without potential critic plateaus near 35%; SFT checkpoint about 31%. Subgoal completion moves from stuck at subgoal 1 (phase 0) to a diagonal chain (phase 6).
limits: Training method; not applicable to a scaffold-only agent. Values read from text describing figures.
agent_relevance: Subgoal progress is a useful dense signal. For a scaffold, count verified subgoals as the progress measure.

source: Shrager, Pitman & Golec (2026) Executable Archaeology: Reanimating Simon's Heuristic Compiler (1961) and KBEmacs (1984)
finding: Reran Simon's 1961 Heuristic Compiler, a GPS-style means-ends program that writes programs, and reproduced the code in Simon's 1963 paper. Simon himself argued in 1984 that means-ends analysis alone was not enough for programming: a system also needs indexed operators and many high-level strategies.
numbers: Reproduced the compiled code appearing in Simon (1963); KBEmacs SQRT self-test reproduced. Reanimation done with an AI coding assistant.
quote: Something like Simon's means-ends loop survives in the harness of such a system
limits: Historical reproduction, not a performance test. Authors state reproducing behaviour does not show the theory is right.
agent_relevance: Means-ends is a loop, not a full solver: it needs a library of operators indexed by the differences they remove (the schema's operator set O1-O8).

source: Wikipedia (accessed 2026) General Problem Solver
finding: GPS (Newell, Shaw, Simon, RAND, late 1950s) separated problem knowledge from solving strategy, built subgoals to close gaps, and solved simple tasks such as Tower of Hanoi. It could not solve real-world problems because the search got lost in combinatorial explosion.
numbers: No quantitative benchmarks given. Article body says 1957, page description says 1959.
quote: could not solve any real-world problems because the search was easily lost in the combinatorial explosion
limits: Secondary source, no inline numbers. Read through a summarising fetch. Primary papers not opened.
agent_relevance: Expect GPS-style loops to fail by blow-up on open problems. Bound depth and prune in code.

source: Wikipedia (accessed 2026) Sussman anomaly
finding: Sussman (thesis, early 1970s; book 1975) showed that planners that pursue goals one at a time without interleaving fail on a three-block problem because each subgoal undoes the other. The core boundary condition of difference reduction.
numbers: Blocks: C on A, B on table; goal A on B on C. Doing 'A on B' first then 'B on C' destroys the first, and the reverse order also fails.
limits: Secondary source with no inline citations (the page itself says so). Read through a summarising fetch.
agent_relevance: Subgoal order matters when goals interact. The agent must test subgoal interaction, not just attack differences in listed order.

source: Valmeekam, Marquez, Sreedharan & Kambhampati (2023) On the Planning Abilities of LLMs: A Critical Investigation (PlanBench)
finding: Autonomous plan generation by GPT-4 is poor on IPC-style domains and collapses when names are obfuscated, which points to pattern matching rather than difference reduction.
numbers: GPT-4 average success about 12% across domains; Blocksworld about 34% (206 and 210 of 600 solved with one-shot and zero-shot natural language); Mystery (obfuscated) Blocksworld 1 of 600, and 0 with random names; GPT-3.5 solved 0 natural-language instances. Chain of thought did little (about the same as one-shot).
quote: whatever accidental planning performance LLMs show is likely connected to pattern matching rather than reasoning
limits: GPT-family only (2023 models), 3-5 blocks. Later reasoning models do far better.
agent_relevance: A fair baseline for any means-ends scaffold: test on obfuscated names so recall cannot help.

source: Valmeekam et al. (2023) PlanBench / LLM-Modulo back-prompting results
finding: With a sound external verifier (VAL) that names the unmet precondition and back-prompts GPT-4, a correct plan appears within 15 rounds for most instances. Verifier-fed repair is far stronger than self-judged repair.
numbers: Instances correct within 15 feedback rounds: Blocksworld 41/50 (82%), Logistics 35/50 (70%), Mystery Blocksworld 5/50 (10%); average rounds for the correct ones about 3.7, 3.3 and 7.0. LLM plan as seed for the LPG planner cut search steps.
limits: Verifier is formal and external; Mystery BW stays hard. Sample of 50 per domain.
agent_relevance: Supports G2: revise from real checker output. The Mystery domain shows repair cannot rescue a poorly understood domain.

source: Kambhampati et al. (2024) Position: LLMs Can't Plan, But Can Help Planning in LLM-Modulo Frameworks
finding: Review of why LLM planning claims fail: the hard part of planning is assembling actions into a plan that handles subgoal and resource interactions. Many positive reports work where subgoal interactions can be ignored or are fixed by a human in the loop.
numbers: No new experiments. Notes ReAct and Reflexion largely ignore subgoal interactions in ALFWorld by focusing on single subgoals or relying on an ergodic world.
quote: many papers claiming LLMs have planning abilities wind up confusing general planning knowledge extracted from the LLMs for executable plans
limits: Position paper by the PlanBench authors; the critique of ToT is argued, not measured here.
agent_relevance: Names the exact boundary of difference reduction: subgoal interaction. Any means-ends claim for our agent needs a test with interacting subgoals.

source: Hao et al. (2023) Reasoning with Language Model is Planning with World Model (RAP)
finding: Monte Carlo tree search over LLM-simulated states with a reward that counts goal conditions met (a difference measure) plus action likelihood. The Blocksworld trace shows the Sussman-type error: CoT satisfies the second goal first and blocks the first, while RAP found the right order by searching.
numbers: Blocksworld success at 2/4/6 steps: CoT (LLaMA-33B) 0.17/0.02/0.00; CoT pass@10 0.23/0.07/0.00; CoT (GPT-4) 0.50/0.63/0.40; RAP(10) 1.00/0.86/0.26; RAP(20) 1.00/0.88/0.42. Average about 64% for RAP vs near-complete failure for CoT.
limits: LLaMA-33B vs GPT-4 comparison across different settings; 6-step still low. Reward design tuned by the authors.
agent_relevance: The goal-conditions-met count is a ready-made, code-checkable difference measure for O5. Search over subgoal order fixes goal-interaction errors that greedy CoT makes.

source: Prasad et al. (2024) ADaPT: As-Needed Decomposition and Planning with Language Models
finding: Recursive decomposition only when the executor fails on a (sub)task: the subgoal-on-failure part of means-ends analysis. It beat ReAct, plan-and-execute and Reflexion with GPT-3.5.
numbers: Success gains: up to 28.3 points on ALFWorld, 27 on WebShop, 33 on TextCraft. ALFWorld: +28.3 over ReAct, +23.8 over Try-Again, +14.1 over Reflexion; WebShop +9 over Reflexion, +6 over LATS; pick2 tasks over 4x. Raising max depth d_max from 1 to 3 raised success on all datasets.
limits: GPT-3.5 completion models; max depth 3 to 4; benefit is larger when the executor is weak (Fig 5).
agent_relevance: Closest published LLM-agent form of recursive subgoaling: decompose on a failure signal, not on a schedule (matches G1).

source: Kazemi et al. (2023) LAMBADA: Backward Chaining for Automated Reasoning in Natural Language
finding: Backward chaining from the goal (select rule, decompose into subgoals, fact check) beats forward chain-of-thought as proof depth grows. Goal-directed search is the logical-reasoning cousin of means-ends analysis.
numbers: Relative accuracy gain at depth 5: ProofWriter-PUD 44% over CoT and 56% over Selection-Inference; PrOntoQA 37% over CoT and 113% over SI; ParaRules 43% over CoT.
limits: Synthetic proof datasets; PaLM-class model in 2022-23; absolute scores not extracted.
agent_relevance: Working backward from the goal prunes the search; supports starting O5 from the goal side when forward options explode.

source: Zhou et al. (2023) Least-to-Most Prompting; Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts
finding: Least-to-most (solve easier subproblems first, feed answers forward) reached at least 99% on every SCAN split with 14 exemplars vs 16% for CoT. Tree of Thoughts with GPT-4 solved 74% of Game of 24 vs 4% for CoT.
numbers: SCAN: >=99% (least-to-most, 14 exemplars) vs 16% (CoT). Game of 24 (arXiv 2305.10601): 74% vs 4% for GPT-4 CoT.
limits: Only abstract and headline lines checked in both papers. Kambhampati et al. argue ToT's gain comes from problem-specific priming.
agent_relevance: Ordering subproblems and searching alternatives both help; neither tests difference reduction directly.

source: Logeswaran et al. (2022) Few-shot Subgoal Planning with Language Models
finding: Language models predict fine-grained subgoal sequences from an instruction and can be reranked with environment information; LLM subgoal proposals help an embodied agent on ALFRED.
numbers: Using the top language-model prediction as is, without environment information, gave 20% success on ALFRED. Other headline numbers in the paper were not extracted.
limits: Only the 20% figure was confirmed from the text. 2022 models; sequence-level subgoals only.
agent_relevance: Raw subgoal proposals need grounding in the real state before they are used.
